data.title:
A PROCESS
NO PRODUCT
*quite fits.*
data.body:
Spreadsheets passed around by email, or the same data typed into two systems. If your team has built workarounds to get through the week, there is usually a tool worth building.

If a product already does the job, I'll say so. Buying is often the better choice.

data.title:
CG-CMS.
*A whole CMS as a Laravel library.*
data.body: Generators for new content types, a page cache that serves from disk, and a command line that lets tools like Claude Code draft content under the same rules as the editor. This site runs on it.

questions.question: Can you connect it to the systems we already use?
questions.answer: Yes. Integrations are a big part of this work: Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Xero, HubSpot, Notion. It's direct API work, not no-code glue.

questions.question: Do I own the code?
questions.answer: Yes. You get the code, the documentation and the accounts at handover. Nothing is locked to me, so another developer could pick it up and carry on.

questions.question: Why Laravel?
questions.answer: It's what I know best, and it suits business systems well: data, users, queues and integrations. Where TypeScript and Node.js fit the job better, I use those instead.

questions.question: What if the scope changes during the build?
questions.answer: It often does, once people start using the first release. The work lands in small releases, so we adjust the next one rather than unpick a finished build, and the change goes into the written scope.

data.title:
START WITH
*the process.*
data.lede: The first call is about who does what and where it slows down. Then a written scope, so we both know what done looks like.
